- **self**: Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD (21/3)

## How it works

- [statement] The 2026 alcohol review explicitly advises that neither alcohol consumption nor smoking can be recommended for PD prevention because of their overall health harms. Apparent inverse epidemiologic associations should not be translated into advice to start either exposure. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13067329/ · keywords: Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD
- [statement] Observational associations require consideration of confounding and reverse causation, including changes in exposure during prodromal PD. Courage-PD used genetic instruments to address these biases and supported an inverse smoking association, while explicitly leaving coffee and alcohol conclusions uncertain because of limited power. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9211765/ · keywords: Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5664303/

## Measurements and reference values

- [statement] Courage-PD estimated OR 0.74 (95% CI 0.60–0.93) for PD per standard-deviation increase in genetically predicted smoking initiation. It found no significant coffee or alcohol association but cautioned that conclusions for those two exposures were limited by insufficient statistical power. MR interpretation depends on valid instrumental-variable assumptions. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9211765/ · keywords: Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD
- [statement] In Café-PD, 121 people with established PD were randomized to caffeine 200 mg twice daily or placebo. Caffeine did not significantly improve the primary motor outcome at six months; early modest sleepiness improvement attenuated over time, and secondary outcomes included slightly worse cognitive scores and increased dyskinesia. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5664303/ · keywords: Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] The 2020 caffeine meta-analysis reported a progression association from cohort endpoints such as dyskinesia, motor fluctuation and levodopa initiation, but explicitly noted that none of its included studies isolated pure caffeine tablets and that an optimal caffeine dose could not be defined. Its pooled progression association should not be treated as randomized evidence of disease modification. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7353179/ · keywords: Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD
- [statement] In a one-year randomized trial in early PD, transdermal nicotine did not slow progression. Of 163 randomized participants, 101 contributed to the primary endpoint; discontinuation and adverse events were important causes of dropout, and application-site skin reactions were common. The result does not support prescribing nicotine to slow established PD. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38320207/ · keywords: Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD
- [statement] A 2026 UK Biobank analysis reported no overall coffee–PD association, but associations differed by CYP1A2 genotype: below 5 cups/day was associated with lower risk in AA carriers, whereas at least 5 cups/day was associated with higher risk in AC and CC carriers. The authors explicitly describe these observational findings as hypothesis-generating and noncausal. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-026-01519-0 · keywords: Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD
- [statement] Lower PD incidence associated with coffee consumption should be distinguished from treating established PD: EPIC4PD observed an inverse risk association, while Café-PD found no clinically important motor benefit from caffeine treatment. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11175631/ · keywords: Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5664303/
- [statement] Alcohol findings in Mendelian randomization studies conflict: Dominguez-Baleon and colleagues reported lower PD risk with genetically predicted alcohol intake (OR 0.79, 95% CI 0.65–0.96), whereas Courage-PD found no significant association (OR 0.68, 95% CI 0.39–1.18) and emphasized insufficient statistical power. Neither result alone establishes a preventive drinking recommendation. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8263722/ · keywords: Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9211765/

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] Prospective observational evidence frequently associates habitual caffeine or coffee consumption with lower incident PD risk: the 2020 cohort meta-analysis reported HR 0.797 (95% CI 0.748–0.849), and EPIC4PD also reported an inverse association. These are risk associations rather than intervention effects. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7353179/ · keywords: Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11175631/
- [statement] In the 2024 EPIC4PD analysis of 184,024 participants, the highest coffee-intake category versus nonconsumption had adjusted HR 0.63 (95% CI 0.46–0.88). Its nested study of 351 incident cases and 351 controls associated higher prediagnostic caffeine, paraxanthine and theophylline with lower subsequent PD risk; adjustment for smoking and alcohol did not substantially change results. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11175631/ · keywords: Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD
- [statement] In Café-PD, caffeine 200 mg twice daily did not improve the six-month motor outcome versus placebo in established PD. Sixty participants received caffeine and 61 placebo; the between-group MDS-UPDRS-III difference was −0.48 points (95% CI −3.21 to 2.25). This treatment result does not test primary prevention. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5664303/ · keywords: Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD
- [statement] The 2023 correction to Hong’s caffeine meta-analysis fixed citation numbers in tables and figures; the authors stated that the scientific conclusions were unaffected. It should be consulted alongside the original meta-analysis rather than described as a retraction. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9919867/ · keywords: Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD
- [statement] Two Mendelian randomization studies reported inverse smoking-related associations with PD, but for different exposures: Courage-PD found an association for genetic liability to smoking initiation, whereas Dominguez-Baleon and colleagues found an association for smoking continuation (current versus former smokers). These estimates do not identify nicotine as the responsible component. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9211765/ · keywords: Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8263722/
- [statement] Nicotine has not demonstrated clinical benefit as a PD treatment: a randomized early-PD trial found that one year of transdermal nicotine did not slow progression, and a 2025 meta-analysis found no significant pooled short- or long-term motor improvement. The meta-analysis includes the trial and is corroborating synthesis rather than an independent replication. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38320207/ · keywords: Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12384040/

## Facts and statements

- [statement] The 2026 UK Biobank analysis reported no overall coffee–PD association in 435,551 participants with 3319 incident cases, whereas EPIC4PD reported an inverse association. The UK analysis reported differing associations by CYP1A2 genotype; these study-specific results should not be collapsed into a universal protective coffee effect. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-026-01519-0 · keywords: Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11175631/
- [statement] In the UK Biobank study, coffee-by-CYP1A2 interaction was significant, but coffee-by-sex and the three-way coffee-by-genotype-by-sex interactions were not statistically significant. Sex-stratified differences therefore require caution. The authors also state that their coffee measure included decaffeinated coffee, preventing isolation of caffeine-specific exposure, and that this observational study does not establish causality. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-026-01519-0 · keywords: Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD
- [statement] Smoking is associated with lower PD incidence in epidemiologic research, and the Courage-PD Mendelian-randomisation analysis also supported an inverse association for genetic liability to smoking initiation. This exposure association does not establish nicotine treatment efficacy. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38320207/ · keywords: Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9211765/
- [statement] The 2025 nicotine meta-analysis of five randomized trials and 346 participants found no significant short- or long-term motor benefit and no significant short-term improvement in daily functioning, cognition or quality of life, with considerable between-study heterogeneity. It does not establish preventive effects before diagnosis. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12384040/ · keywords: Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD
- [statement] Alcohol–PD findings disagree across study designs and reference groups: NeuroEPIC4PD reported no overall baseline or lifetime alcohol association, whereas the 2026 systematic review reported inverse associations in several pooled observational comparisons and inconsistent MR evidence. Neither result establishes that starting alcohol prevents PD. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7496254/ · keywords: Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13067329/
- [statement] The early-PD nicotine trial randomized 163 participants, but only 101 were assessed for the primary endpoint; discontinuation and adverse events contributed to dropout, and patch-site skin adverse effects were common. Attrition limits interpretation of the efficacy estimate. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38320207/ · keywords: Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD

## Research summary — Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD

Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol require separate interpretations for PD incidence and treatment after diagnosis. Several cohorts associate caffeine or coffee with lower PD risk, but a large UK Biobank analysis found no overall association and reported genotype heterogeneity; caffeine did not improve motor outcomes in Café-PD. Smoking has an inverse epidemiologic association, with supportive but assumption-dependent Mendelian-randomisation evidence, while nicotine trials have not demonstrated clinical benefit. Alcohol findings vary between prospective cohorts, pooled observational analyses and genetic studies. These associations do not justify starting smoking or alcohol for prevention, or prescribing nicotine for PD progression. Key uncertainties include reverse causation, confounding, exposure definitions, genotype subgroup replication and whether any intervention before diagnosis changes incidence.

## Source disagreement — Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD

The 2026 UK Biobank analysis reported no overall coffee–PD association in 435,551 participants with 3319 incident cases, whereas EPIC4PD reported an inverse association. The UK analysis reported differing associations by CYP1A2 genotype; these study-specific results should not be collapsed into a universal protective coffee effect.

## Source disagreement — Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD

Alcohol–PD findings disagree across study designs and reference groups: NeuroEPIC4PD reported no overall baseline or lifetime alcohol association, whereas the 2026 systematic review reported inverse associations in several pooled observational comparisons and inconsistent MR evidence. Neither result establishes that starting alcohol prevents PD.
